prompt: A Fargate service must accept port 80 only from inside the VPC. Where is that rule written?
hint: In awsvpc mode, what carries the network interface?

choices.text: On the security group of the instance the tasks run on
choices.why: There is no instance of yours; the host is AWS's.

choices.text: In the task definition's portMappings
choices.why: portMappings opens the container's port; it says nothing about who may reach it.

choices.text: On a security group the tasks carry
choices.why: Each task has its own interface, and the group named in the network configuration is on it.

choices.text: In the cluster's settings, for every task in it
choices.why: Clusters carry no network rules; each service or task names its own groups.

prompt: A /23 subnet has 512 addresses, and AWS reserves five in every subnet. With nothing else in it, how many Fargate tasks can it hold at most?
hint: One private address per task.

prompt: A Fargate task in a private subnet, with assignPublicIp DISABLED, no NAT gateway and no VPC endpoints, stops with CannotPullContainerError. What fixes it?
hint: The task has to reach the registry before it can start.

choices.text: A route to a NAT gateway, or endpoints for ECR, CloudWatch Logs and S3
choices.why: Either gives the task a way to the registry and to the logs without a public address.

choices.text: Opening port 443 inbound on the task's security group
choices.why: The pull is outbound; an inbound rule does not create a route.

choices.text: Giving the execution role ecr:BatchGetImage
choices.why: A permission is no use without a network path to the registry, and the error is about reaching it.

choices.text: Switching the task to bridge network mode
choices.why: Fargate accepts awsvpc only.

prompt: moto's run-task in awsvpc mode failed with a 500, and describe-network-interfaces then showed one interface described as moto ECS. What does that interface stand for?
hint: Which part of a task's launch did moto get through before it failed?

choices.text: A leftover from the lab's VPC, unrelated to the task
choices.why: It is in the task's subnet with the task's security group, created by the run-task call.

choices.text: The task's own network interface, the piece of awsvpc that moto did create
choices.why: On AWS the same interface is listed in the task's attachments and deleted when the task stops.

choices.text: The NAT gateway the task would use to pull its image
choices.why: A NAT gateway is a separate resource; nothing here created one.

choices.text: An interface of the container instance hosting the task
choices.why: There is no container instance on Fargate.

prompt: Two Fargate tasks of the same service both listen on port 80, and AWS happens to start them on the same physical host. What happens?
hint: In awsvpc, whose address is the port opened on?

choices.text: The second fails with RESOURCE:PORTS, as in lesson 8
choices.why: That was a fixed hostPort on a shared instance address; here each task has its own address.

choices.text: Both run, each on port 80 of its own address
choices.why: Each task has its own interface, so their ports never meet.

choices.text: Fargate moves the second to port 81
choices.why: Nothing renumbers the port; it does not need to.

choices.text: Docker's bridge shares port 80 between them
choices.why: There is no bridge in awsvpc mode, and a port is never shared.

prompt: The only network mode a Fargate task definition may use is ___.
hint: Each task gets its own interface in the VPC.

prompt: A Fargate task on x86 reserves 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB. At 0.0696 USD per vCPU-hour and 0.0076 per GB-hour, what does it cost for a month of 730 hours, in USD, to the cent?
hint: vCPU times its meter, plus GB times its meter, then times 730.

prompt: A cache needs 4 GB of memory and very little CPU. What is the smallest Fargate size that holds it?
hint: Memory ranges rise with the CPU.

choices.text: 0.25 vCPU with 4 GB
choices.why: 256 CPU units allow at most 2 GB; moto accepted it and AWS refuses it.

choices.text: 1 vCPU with 4 GB
choices.why: It fits, and pays for twice the CPU of a smaller size that also fits.

choices.text: 2 vCPU with 4 GB, the lowest memory that size allows
choices.why: Valid, and four times the CPU the cache needs.

choices.text: 0.5 vCPU with 4 GB
choices.why: 512 units allow 1 to 4 GB, so this is the first row that reaches 4.

prompt: fargate_cost.py put two tasks of 1 vCPU and 2 GB at 123.81 USD a month on x86 and 99.19 on Arm. How much a year does moving them to Arm save, in USD, to the cent?
hint: The monthly difference, twelve times.

prompt: A task reserves 1 vCPU and uses a tenth of it all day. What does Fargate bill for its CPU?
hint: Fargate meters the definition, not the load.

choices.text: A tenth of a vCPU-hour per hour
choices.why: Fargate does not meter use; what is reserved is what is billed.

choices.text: 1 vCPU-hour per hour, the whole reservation
choices.why: The bill follows cpu in the task definition, by the second, used or not.

choices.text: Nothing until it passes 50% of its reservation
choices.why: There is no such threshold; billing starts with the image download.

choices.text: The instance it runs on, shared with other tasks
choices.why: No instance appears on a Fargate bill.

prompt: Which of these appear on a Fargate bill? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two meters, and one more for disk past a threshold.

choices.text: vCPU-hours the task definitions reserve
choices.why: One of the two meters.

choices.text: GB-hours of memory the task definitions reserve
choices.why: The other meter.

choices.text: Ephemeral storage above the first 20 GB
choices.why: 0.000211 USD per GB-hour on the sheet.

choices.text: A charge for ECS itself, per cluster
choices.why: ECS has no charge of its own, on EC2 or on Fargate.

choices.text: The hours of the hosts AWS runs the tasks on
choices.why: Those hosts are AWS's; their cost is inside the two meters.

prompt: An m7i.large container instance costs 117.27 USD a month; two Fargate tasks with the same 2 vCPUs cost 123.81. When is the instance the cheaper choice?
hint: The instance is billed full or empty.

choices.text: Always, because it is cheaper per hour
choices.why: Only while it is full; an instance a third empty costs the same.

choices.text: Never, because Fargate has no instance to pay for
choices.why: Fargate's meters include the host's cost; full, the instance wins.

choices.text: When it stays nearly full all month, patching aside
choices.why: Packed, it is cheaper and has twice the memory; the spare room a cluster keeps erodes that.

choices.text: Only on Arm
choices.why: The comparison here is x86 against x86; Arm lowers both sides.

prompt: A service's strategy is base=1 on FARGATE, weight 1 on FARGATE and weight 3 on FARGATE_SPOT. With 9 tasks, how many run on FARGATE?
hint: The base first, then one in four of the rest.

prompt: AWS reclaims the capacity under a Fargate Spot task. What does the container's main process receive first?
hint: The same thing any stopped task receives.

choices.text: SIGKILL, because the capacity is gone
choices.why: SIGKILL comes only after stopTimeout, if the process is still running.

choices.text: SIGTERM, with stopTimeout to finish before SIGKILL
choices.why: That window, up to 120 seconds on Fargate, is the whole warning the code gets.

choices.text: An HTTP request to a notice path
choices.why: The EventBridge event goes outside the task; the process itself gets a signal.

choices.text: Nothing; the task disappears
choices.why: The task is stopped the ordinary way, signal first.

prompt: What is the longest stopTimeout a Fargate container definition may set?
hint: It matches the length of Spot's warning.

choices.text: 10 seconds, Docker's default
choices.why: That is docker stop's default on a laptop; ECS's default is 30.

choices.text: 30 seconds
choices.why: That is the default, not the ceiling.

choices.text: 120 seconds
choices.why: Two minutes, the whole of the warning.

choices.text: 15 minutes
choices.why: No container gets that long to stop on Fargate.

prompt: A stopped Spot task's container reports exit code 137. What happened?
hint: 137 is 128 plus a signal number.

choices.text: The handler finished and exited cleanly
choices.why: A clean exit is 0, as the first run showed.

choices.text: The image could not be pulled
choices.why: A task that never started has no container exit code.

choices.text: It ran out of memory, which is exit 137 by definition
choices.why: An OOM kill is also a SIGKILL; with Spot and a short timeout, the timeout is the likelier cause, and the stopped reason tells them apart.

choices.text: It was killed with SIGKILL, signal 9, still running at stopTimeout
choices.why: The process did not finish inside the timeout, as the five-second run showed.

prompt: Put what happens to a well-written worker on Fargate Spot, when AWS reclaims its capacity, in order.
hint: The signal comes before the kill, and the replacement last.
items: AWS decides to take the capacity back
The container's main process receives SIGTERM
The handler saves its work and exits inside stopTimeout
The service starts a replacement task
trap: The replacement does not wait in advance: the service only starts one once the task is gone.

prompt: Why did the SIGTERM runs pass --stop-signal SIGTERM to docker run?
hint: Look at what docker image inspect printed.

choices.text: Docker sends SIGKILL unless told otherwise
choices.why: Docker sends SIGTERM, or the image's own stop signal when it names one.

choices.text: The nginx image names SIGQUIT as its stop signal
choices.why: Without the flag the shell would have received SIGQUIT and its TERM handler would never have run.

choices.text: Fargate requires it in the task definition
choices.why: It is a docker run flag here, not a Fargate setting.

choices.text: A shell ignores SIGTERM unless the flag is set
choices.why: The trap is what makes the shell handle it; the flag only chooses which signal Docker sends.

prompt: Match each need to what Fargate offers for it.
hint: Each answer replaces something the instance used to provide.

pairs.left: A shell to look inside a running task
A log shipper beside every task
pairs.right: A sidecar container in the task definition
An EFS file system mounted into it

prompt: moto stored a Fargate definition that asked for bridge mode as awsvpc. Why is that worse than a refusal?
hint: Compare what the author wrote with what reading it back says.

choices.text: Because awsvpc costs more than bridge
choices.why: The network mode does not change the Fargate price.

choices.text: Because the definition read back says something its author never wrote
choices.why: A refusal points at the mistake; a silent rewrite hides it until AWS refuses the file.

choices.text: Because AWS would also rewrite it, so the error is hidden twice
choices.why: AWS refuses bridge for Fargate at registration.

choices.text: Because bridge tasks cannot reach the internet
choices.why: Bridge works on EC2; the point is what moto did to the file.

prompt: A Fargate task writes uploads to its own disk, and the task is replaced during a deployment. What happens to the files?
hint: Where does the 20 GB live?

choices.text: They are copied to the replacement
choices.why: Nothing copies ephemeral storage between tasks.

choices.text: They are gone with the task
choices.why: Ephemeral storage lives on capacity the task gives back, like lesson 3's instance store.

choices.text: They move to S3 automatically
choices.why: Fargate writes nothing to S3 for you; that is the application's job.

choices.text: They stay on the host until the next task
choices.why: The host is AWS's and is not handed to your next task.

prompt: Which of these workloads cannot move from ECS on EC2 to Fargate as it stands?
hint: Find the one that needs the host itself.

choices.text: A web API behind a load balancer
choices.why: That is Fargate's most common use.

choices.text: A nightly batch job of 20 minutes
choices.why: A run-task on Fargate suits it.

choices.text: A container that loads a kernel module, run privileged
choices.why: privileged is refused on Fargate, because it would control a host that is not yours.

choices.text: A queue worker that reads from SQS
choices.why: It needs a task role and nothing from the host.

prompt: A worker on Fargate Spot takes about five minutes per message and cannot resume halfway. What makes interruptions safe?
hint: 120 seconds is less than five minutes.

choices.text: On SIGTERM, stop taking messages and let the unfinished one become visible again
choices.why: The message goes back to the queue and another worker does it whole; nothing is half done.

choices.text: Raise stopTimeout to 300 seconds
choices.why: Fargate allows at most 120.

choices.text: Ignore SIGTERM so the work is not interrupted
choices.why: SIGKILL arrives at stopTimeout anyway, mid-message.

choices.text: Put base=0 so every task is on Spot
choices.why: That makes interruptions more frequent, not safer.

prompt: A private subnet has interface endpoints for ECR and CloudWatch Logs and no NAT gateway, and Fargate tasks still fail to pull their image. What is the likeliest gap?
hint: Where does ECR keep the image layers?

choices.text: The task needs a public IP to use endpoints
choices.why: Endpoints exist precisely so that private tasks need none.

choices.text: The execution role lacks logs:PutLogEvents
choices.why: That would fail the logs, not the pull.

choices.text: A gateway endpoint for S3
choices.why: The layers come from S3, so without that endpoint the download has no path.

choices.text: The cluster has no FARGATE capacity provider
choices.why: That would stop the task being placed, not its image being pulled.
